conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You're here because of nausea and vomiting that started this morning, is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I was eating cereal with milk, and suddenly I felt very sick and vomited a few times.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. This feels similar to your past gastroparesis flares, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. It’s been years since I’ve had one this bad. I’ve been managing well with diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re on a J-tube for meds only, not feeding, and you’ve been eating normally otherwise?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I use the J-tube just for my medications. I haven’t needed tube feeding in years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good. We’ve reviewed your labs from the ER. Your white blood cell count is elevated at 12.5, but you don’t have a fever or signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? I had high white counts last time too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s likely a stress response from the flare. Since you’re not running a fever and feel better after treatment, we don’t think it’s an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. I did get Zofran and fluids in the ER and started feeling better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll continue IV fluids and anti-nausea meds. We also did a J-tube study to make sure it’s in good position.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And is it okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the tube is patent and in the right place—tip in the duodenum, with contrast flowing into the jejunum. No issues there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to hear. I was worried it might be blocked or moved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of that. We’ll keep you NPO for now and slowly advance your diet tomorrow if you stay symptom-free.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How are you feeling today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Much better. I haven’t felt nauseous since last night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your repeat labs this morning show your white count has dropped to 7.2, which is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a big improvement. What about the other labs?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your electrolytes are stable. We also checked your thyroid function—your TSH is 4.3, which is a bit high.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m on levothyroxine. Wasn’t it normal last time?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it was normal during your last admission. The elevated TSH now might be contributing to your gastroparesis flare.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So could my thyroid be making my stomach worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, hypothyroidism can slow digestion. We’re increasing your levothyroxine from 100 to 125 mcg daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll take it in the morning on an empty stomach, like always.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll also start you on a clear liquid diet and see how you tolerate it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: How’s the clear liquid diet going?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No nausea. I had broth and apple juice, and I feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. We’ll advance you to a soft, low-fat diet for dinner.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated the soft diet well. No vomiting or discomfort?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: None at all. I even had a small portion of mashed potatoes and chicken.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow morning if you continue to do well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What should I do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue small, low-fat, low-dairy meals. Avoid large portions. Stick to your meds, especially the new thyroid dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I consider using the J-tube for feeding again?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s something to discuss with your GI doctor. Since your tube is working, using it a few days a week might help prevent future flares.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. Vital signs are stable, you’ve eaten a regular diet, and labs are normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready to go home. Thank you for helping me through this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re discharging you with instructions to follow up with your PCP in 6 weeks to check your TSH.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my gastroenterologist for the J-tube feeding discussion?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, exactly. Call us if nausea returns or you can’t keep fluids down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Dr. Lee.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. You’re cleared to go home now.
